Multi-view 3D reconstruction

From Photographs to a Measurable 3D Model

Reconstructing the three dimensional shape and appearance of a real object from nothing but photographs.

01

Starting from the photographs, a traditional reconstruction recovers a first, sparse 3D shape.

02

A learned multi-view depth model, CasDiffMVS, densifies it into a fuller 3D representation.

03

3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a photorealistic, free-viewpoint model that can be rotated and viewed from any angle.

The work

This work turns a set of ordinary photographs of an object into a detailed three dimensional model, one that can be viewed, measured, and explored from every side. No specialized scanner is required, and nothing needs to touch the object, since a set of overlapping photographs is enough. The aim is to recover the shape of a real part as faithfully as a camera can capture it, so that the same images used to document an object can also help reveal its geometry.

The reconstruction is built in stages, and each stage adds more than the one before it. It begins with a traditional reconstruction that estimates the object's shape from the overlapping views, producing a first, sparse result. A cross-view consistency step then improves that reconstruction, keeping only the points that several photographs independently agree on and removing the unstable geometry that ordinary reconstruction can introduce. To recover a fuller surface, a learned multi-view depth model, CasDiffMVS, estimates depth across the views and densifies the result, turning the sparse outline into a far more complete model. Finally, 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a photorealistic, free-viewpoint model from the same photographs, producing a lifelike result that can be rotated and examined from any direction.

For manufacturing, this approach points toward a practical, camera-based way to inspect parts. The same photographs that document a part on the line can also support its inspection, by comparing the reconstructed shape against the intended design and helping reveal surface defects or variations from it. Because the result is a three dimensional model rather than a flat image, it can support measurement and be kept as a clear visual record, a digital twin that can be revisited or shared long after the part has moved on. The lifelike, rotatable model adds a further benefit, because an inspector can orbit the part on screen and study every surface and angle remotely, without needing the part in hand. In place of slow manual measurement or specialized scanning hardware, a team can work from cameras it already has, a more accessible and contact-free way to understand the parts it makes.
